description: We're the robotics team from Al-Bayan Bilingual School (BBS) in Kuwait, with experience competing in national and international robotics Olympiads. We've spent years building and programming robots for competitions and are now taking on a different kind of challenge. For NASA Space Apps 2026 we're working on Flame in Freefall to explore how AI can help researchers better understand combustion in space and improve spacecraft fire safety.
summary:
FLARE is an interactive research platform designed to make NASA's microgravity combustion research more accessible, comparable, and useful for future space exploration.

Our platform integrates 19 NASA combustion investigations and 1,981 structured experimental table records from NASA's Physical Science Informatics repository. Through an interactive investigation explorer, researchers can examine experimental conditions, compare scientific findings, and visualize the relationships between oxygen concentration and atmospheric pressure.

FLARE also features a mission scenario tool that ranks relevant NASA investigations for proposed spacecraft environments, alongside an AI research assistant designed to provide evidence-grounded scientific explanations.

By connecting research on fire prevention, detection, and suppression, FLARE helps users identify relevant experimental evidence and important research gaps. Rather than making unsupported predictions, our platform emphasizes scientific transparency, source traceability, and the limitations of applying microgravity findings to lunar and Martian environments.

Our goal is to transform complex NASA research into accessible insights that can support safer human space exploration.
details:
Flame in Freefall turns NASA's Physical Science Informatics (PSI)
archive of microgravity combustion research into fire-safety answers
for crewed habitats such as spacecraft, lunar and Martian bases, and
pressurized rovers. It indexes the 19 PSI combustion investigations
that flew as experiments, which together hold 1,981 parsed tests and
264 linked publications, and presents them on six public pages with no
login. The Explorer lets you search and filter the investigations by
fire-safety pillar, fuel, hardware, and oxygen, pressure and airflow
ranges, and export the matching test rows as CSV or JSON. Its home
page opens with a "golden record" where each groove is one
investigation, each tick is an oxygen level it actually tested, and
lines across it mark real habitat atmospheres. Each investigation has
its own page with its objective, tested conditions, key findings with
verbatim source quotes, test rows, materials, data gaps and
publications. The Condition Space chart plots every test that records
both oxygen and pressure against sourced reference atmospheres such as
Earth sea level, the ISS cabin, the EVA spacesuit and NASA's
recommended 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen exploration atmosphere. The Scenario
page takes a habitat's oxygen, pressure, gravity, airflow and material
and ranks every investigation with a fixed, fully explained score. The
Compare page shows two to four investigations side by side with their
differences highlighted, and an AI assistant answers plain-language
questions by looking up the dataset and citing the investigations it
used.

Under the hood, our code pulls investigation records and
experimental-table CSV files from PSI's public API and parses them
into structured tests. Every number traces back to its source cell,
and unknown values stay empty and are shown as "not available" rather
than estimated. Investigation-level facts were extracted by an LLM
agent, reviewed by two more, and then re-verified by code, with an
automated audit that rechecks 765 quotes and 13,447 numbers against
their sources. The scenario ranking uses no AI at all. A missing value
scores zero and is labelled as missing, so an investigation with
sparse data cannot rank highly by default. The assistant uses Claude
with four lookup tools that search tests, fetch an investigation, rank
a scenario and search publications. Our code performs every lookup and
calculation, while Claude chooses which tools to call, writes the
answer, cites its sources and says so when the data does not cover a
question.

NASA's combustion data covers decades of flight experiments, but it is
scattered across records, tables and papers that are hard to find,
compare or interpret. Flame in Freefall brings it into one place,
shows which tests ran near a given habitat atmosphere, and is open
about where the data has gaps. We want habitat designers, fire-safety
engineers and students to be able to ask what is actually known about
fire at 34% oxygen and 8.2 psia and get a sourced answer in seconds,
so that the next lunar base or rover is designed on evidence.

The project is written in TypeScript using Next.js 16, React 19 and
Tailwind CSS 4, with Zod for data validation, Vitest for 83 unit
tests, csv-parse for reading NASA's tables and the Anthropic
TypeScript SDK for the Claude-powered assistant, and it is deployed on
Vercel. The charts are hand-built SVG, and no special hardware was
used.

What makes the project creative is how it presents the data. Instead
of a generic dashboard, the home page shows the archive as a golden
record in the spirit of the Voyager record, where the grooves and
ticks are the real data and the habitat atmospheres radiate across
them like the pulsar map on the record's cover. The assistant is also
held to the data in an unusual way as it can only answer through lookups
over the same dataset the rest of the site shows, so its answers agree
with the charts and rankings.

We weighed several factors throughout. The first was scientific
honesty. Every indexed test ran in microgravity and PSI holds no lunar
or Mars-gravity combustion data, so the site presents microgravity
results as the closest available reference points for those
environments, never as bounds or predictions. We also required
traceability, meaning no invented numbers, a verbatim source quote
behind every claim and clear labelling of anything an AI extracted,
and we show values only at the precision their sources give.
Accessibility mattered too so the site supports keyboard navigation,
offers a table view of every chart value, encodes categories by shape
as well as color and respects reduced motion settings. Finally, we
kept it open so anyone can use the site without an account and download
the data.
